challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: the hint names hth2020-private; `cloud_enum -k hth2020-private` reports OPEN S3 BUCKET, then `curl http://hth2020-private.s3.amazonaws.com/flag.txt` returns HTH{checkthisoffyourbucketlist}. The same post's OhSnap! step reads the bucket's `?versions` listing, revealing the key and timestamp of a deleted object

read and confirmed: bucket listing permission set to Everyone; `aws s3 ls s3://flaws.cloud/ --no-sign-request --region us-west-2` lists the objects, then `aws s3 cp s3://flaws.cloud/secret-dd02c7c.html --no-sign-request --region us-west-2` downloads the next-stage artefact. Level 2 (Any Authenticated AWS User) is the credential-gated exception, level 3 adds git-history analysis after an anonymous `s3 sync`

positives: the bucket serves a listing and object bodies to a caller with no credentials at all; the solve is a read, not an exploit
region discovery precedes any permission judgement: HEAD on the bucket exposes x-amz-bucket-region even behind a 403, and a 301 PermanentRedirect is a wrong-region answer rather than a denial
the artefact is fetched with a plain unauthenticated GET (`curl`) or `aws s3 cp --no-sign-request`; nothing is signed and no account exists
a denied listing does not close the challenge: the legacy `?versions` listing names deleted objects and a direct object GET still returns 200
negatives: an ACL scoped to Any Authenticated AWS User (flAWS level 2): an AWS account is required, so the exposure is credential-gated, not anonymous
a public EBS snapshot or an open Lambda/API Gateway stage that reveals the flag — no bucket read is involved (CTFTTE-CLD-004/006 territory)
a bucket read performed with keys recovered earlier in the challenge: the read is then a consequence of IAM access, which is CTFTTE-CLD-002
directory brute-forcing against an HTTP origin (CTFTTE-WEB-001) even when the hostname contains `s3`
boundaries: distinct from CTFTTE-CLD-002: there the bucket is read with valid credentials and the weakness is the permission set; here no credential exists
distinct from CTFTTE-CLD-003: an SSRF into IMDS retrieves credentials, not objects
flAWS level 3 is the bridge case — anonymous listing exposes a git repository whose history leaks keys; only the listing is CLD-001, the rest is CLD-002
GCS and Azure Blob reproduce the same pattern with a different response shape (EnumerationResults JSON/XML): same technique, different parser

external_mappings.justification: Data from Cloud Storage Object is the exact behaviour; CTFT adds the anonymous-enumeration craft (name permutations, region discovery, versions listing) that ATT&CK omits.
Cloud Storage Object Discovery describes the enumeration step that precedes the read.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: sha256crypt hash extracted from an embedded device, hashcat -m 7400 against rockyou, then a rule-based pass
read and confirmed: Kerberoast TGS-REP hash, hashcat -m 13100 against seclists, Status: Cracked

positives: the challenge yields a hash in a documented format and the flag is the plaintext behind it (sha256crypt $5$, Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23)
the constraint is the candidate space, not the algorithm: mode selection plus the right wordlist or rule set is the whole solve
a rule pass (best64) or a themed wordlist succeeds where a plain wordlist exhausts
negatives: online credential brute-force against a login form (hydra against http-post-form) — no hash is ever recovered, the oracle is the application
a hash whose plaintext is irrelevant because the challenge only needs the hash as an identifier
recovering a key by exploiting the cipher's structure rather than by search — that is CTFTTE-CRY-001 or CTFTTE-CRY-003
boundaries: distinct from CTFTTE-CRY-001 (weak RSA parameters): there the key falls to arithmetic, here only to search
distinct from CTFTTE-CRY-004 (nonce reuse): no cryptanalytic relation is exploited
online brute-force is NOT this technique and has no CTFT entry yet — see the candidate list in TODO.md

external_mappings.justification: Password Cracking is the exact ATT&CK behaviour; CTFT adds the mode-selection and wordlist-constraint craft ATT&CK omits.
Use of a password hash with insufficient computational effort is what makes the search tractable.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: a single PCAP carries five questions; the asset naming convention and the target hostname are recovered from the scan traffic
read and confirmed: tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http reassembles the transferred objects that carry the flag

positives: the payload exists only as a reassembled stream or exported object, never in a single packet
the capture is legitimate traffic and the concealment is dilution: the answer is one conversation among many
the solve is a reassembly and export operation, not a decode of one field
negatives: a flag readable in a single packet payload with `strings` — no reassembly is required
a link to a packet-capture resource or a mention of pcap tooling in a threat-intel note — describing the format is not exercising the technique
a covert channel in protocol header fields, which is CTFTTE-NET-006
boundaries: distinct from CTFTTE-NET-007 (packet-capture forensics maze): NET frames the network puzzle, FOR frames artifact reassembly from the capture
distinct from CTFTTE-NET-002 (DNS covert channel): there the carrier is the protocol, here the carrier is the stream
distinct from CTFTTE-STE-002 (appended data): the container is a capture, not a file with trailing bytes

external_mappings.justification: Application Layer Protocol is the carrier ATT&CK models; ATT&CK omits the reassembly and export craft that defines the CTF technique.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: the door is /hackfest-schedule, a linked page whose night-scene decor contains an interactive computer activated with 'Press E'; activation then loads hf-schedule-fx.json and the terminal scripts

positives: the route is public and linked; the gate is an interaction inside the page scene, not a hidden path
the decisive signal is a per-page asset inventory: the interaction-only loader and its unique assets surface by rarity, not by keyword
activating the object unlocks a multi-stage chain whose next surfaces only exist after the interaction
negatives: an unlinked route found by fuzzing — that is CTFTTE-WEB-001, no interaction is required
an asset that loads on page load and merely looks interactive — the gate must be the interaction
a keyboard shortcut documented for a real OS or a genuine easter egg without a challenge surface
boundaries: distinct from CTFTTE-WEB-001 (obscured endpoint): the route is linked and public; only the interactive object is hidden
distinct from CTFTTE-WEB-018 (interaction-gated asset loading): GAM-007 frames the hidden object itself, WEB-018 frames the deferred loading mechanism
distinct from CTFTTE-GAM-008 (simulated OS stage): the stage is the machine's internals; this entry is the gate that reveals it

external_mappings.justification: Hide Artifacts is the closest echo; ATT&CK has no browser-interaction trigger for disclosure.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: KiCad 6.0.9 Gerber package of a sabotaged HadesMicro flight controller; extra copper text strokes on B_Cu (vertical, 0.25 mm, reads HTB{533_7h3_1nn32_w02k1n95 at 270 deg unmirrored) and on inner layer In1_Cu (horizontal, 0.20 mm, reads _0f_313c720n1c5#$@}); flag submitted and accepted. Reproduced 2026-10-22 with FOM tools/scripts/gerber-layer-inspect.py (hunt: exactly 2 clusters, 0 false positives; diff vs upstream pms67/HadesFCS: only these 2 additions)

positives: the payload is geometry (stroked copper text) inside Gerber fabrication files and exists only once coordinates are plotted; strings/grep on the plain-text files reveal nothing
the hiding place is a layer invisible on the finished board (inner copper In1_Cu) or one the composite render does not isolate, so a per-layer view is mandatory
the payload strokes form connected components touching no pad, via or pour, which makes them separable from real traces without any reference design
the challenge story names a modified open-source design, so the upstream Gerbers serve as a diff baseline
negatives: a flag in firmware/EEPROM dumped over UART/JTAG/SPI from a physical or emulated device (CTFTTE-HWR-002): the evidence is executable content, not plotted geometry
a flag in the board's silkscreen/fab text that is plainly visible in a composite render: no layer-level concealment
a schematic/netlist puzzle where the secret is a logic function of the circuit rather than drawn geometry
boundaries: single event so far (one challenge, replayed): not yet attested, which needs >= 2 independent events
split payloads across layers need ordering by flag delimiters; one fragment alone can look complete
cross-version diffs are noisy (KiCad 5 strokes zone fills, KiCad 6 emits G36 regions): only large ADDED clusters are signal
synonyms: hidden text in PCB inner layer

external_mappings.justification: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain covers tampering with hardware before delivery; CTFT adds the per-layer plotting and reference-diff recovery ATT&CK omits.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed statically: APK and IPA both ship a Hermes bytecode bundle (version 96) behind a generated Expo shell, so platform decompilation shows no application logic; hermes-dec recovered the entry module and the two unsigned GET endpoints it builds from a constant base URL. FLAG NOT VALIDATED - the challenge infrastructure was decommissioned before the replay, so the requests were reconstructed and never sent

positives: the application logic is absent from the platform artifact: decompiling the package yields only the framework bootstrap, which is the signal rather than a dead end
the code ships as a separate compiled asset that starts with an engine bytecode magic and carries a version field
the bytecode version, not the app version, decides whether a decompiler produces code or plausible-looking nonsense
decompilation restores module boundaries and original function names, which is what makes the network surface readable
negatives: logic hidden in a native shared library, where the recovery is reversing the .so (CTFTTE-MOB-002)
renamed or obfuscated DEX bytecode, where the code is readable but mislabelled (CTFTTE-MOB-004)
a hardcoded secret sitting in resources or strings, with no logic to recover (CTFTTE-MOB-001)
a compiled artifact of the same language as its source, where one decompiler suffices and no container triage is needed (CTFTTE-REV-007)
boundaries: single event, and no flag validated: the requests were reconstructed from the bundle, never replayed - attested would need two independent events plus a confirmed solve
the class is stated per engine, not per framework: a different engine keeps the technique and changes the magic, the version table and the decompiler
once the logic is readable the endpoints it reveals belong to the network/web domains; this entry stops at recovering the behaviour
synonyms: logic hidden in an app bundle asset

external_mappings.justification: Compiled-artifact delivery hides the logic from platform tooling; ATT&CK does not model the engine/version triage the recovery depends on.

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: Ghidra shows unreferenced deactivate_camera() printing flag.txt (win function), investigate() reads 0x108 bytes into a 64-byte stack buffer, No PIE/No canary; payload redirects the saved return address to 0x401165. Reproduced locally with GhidraMCP decompilation on 2026-10-15 (fhp).

positives: a flag-printing function exists in the binary but has zero callers (confirmed via cross-references), so reaching it requires control-flow hijack
an unchecked read (264 bytes) into a small stack buffer with No PIE and No canary makes the saved return address directly overwritable
the whole exploit is one payload: fill buffer, saved rbp, then the fixed win-function address (no leak, no ROP)
negatives: ROP chains or ret2libc when the win function is missing - that is CTFTTE-PWN-004 territory
stack canary/PIE present - that is CTFTTE-PWN-006 (leak first)
format-string-driven leaks or writes - that is CTFTTE-PWN-002

challenges.extracted_from: read and confirmed: official write-up loads signal.cf32 (raw IQ, no stated sample rate or centre) in inspectrum, thresholds the amplitude plot into ASK/OOK symbols, recognises Manchester (no run longer than two symbols), keeps every other bit and converts to hex/ASCII after a preamble and sync word; the PDF opens with the flag HTB{RF_H4ck1n6_1s_c00l!!!}. Reproduced 2026-10-25 with .agents/ctf/ctf-sdr/scripts/ook_decode.py (auto carrier -226.1 kHz, 521 symbols, Manchester phase 0 G.E. Thomas, 32-bit 0xAA preamble, flag recovered) and HTB_RF/solve_rflag.py; the 439 us symbol unit holds only under the assumed 2.048 MS/s

positives: a single narrow carrier keyed fully on and off (amplitude only), story about a remote, key fob or garage door
inside the burst no run exceeds two symbol units, the Manchester signature; decoding keeps one symbol per pair
decoded stream starts with a 1010... preamble (0xAA bytes) and a fixed sync word before the flag bytes
negatives: FSK/PSK/QAM where the modulation itself must be recovered (CTFTTE-SDR-001)
a standard protocol with its own decoder and checksum such as POCSAG, AX.25 or ADS-B (CTFTTE-SDR-004)
an IoT stack where pairing keys or a Zigbee/BLE layer are the barrier (CTFTTE-IOT-005)
tones or spectrogram art already in an audio file (CTFTTE-STE-003 / CTFTTE-STE-010)
boundaries: single event so far: not attested, which needs >= 2 independent events
absolute timings depend on the assumed sample rate; the symbol/bit decode is rate-independent

the capture is a saturated 8-bit recording converted to cf32 (256 levels, about 41 % of I/Q values on the -1.0 / +0.992 rails); saturation does not hurt OOK decoding but breaks amplitude-based analyses
Manchester convention and pair phase are ambiguous: all four combinations must be tried and scored

external_mappings.justification: Data Encoding covers reversible encodings of transmitted data; CTFT adds the RF physical layer (envelope slicing, symbol clock recovery) ATT&CK omits.
